promptText: What determines whether a follower replica is currently a member of a partition's in-sync replica (ISR) set?
options: Whether it has fetched from the leader within replica.lag.time.max.ms
Whether it has the exact same replication factor configured as the leader
Whether it is the preferred leader for that partition
Whether it has acknowledged the most recent acks=1 write
explanation: A follower stays in the ISR only as long as it keeps fetching from the leader within the replica.lag.time.max.ms window; falling behind that window drops it from the ISR regardless of replication factor or leadership status.

promptText: With producer setting acks=1, in which scenario can a message the producer believes was successfully sent actually be lost?
options: The leader crashes before any follower has replicated the message
The producer's network connection experiences a brief blip during the send
A follower falls out of the ISR after the leader has already acknowledged the write
The consumer commits its offset before finishing processing the message
explanation: acks=1 only waits for the leader to write the message to its own log, not for follower replication, so a leader crash before followers catch up loses the message even though the producer already received a success response.

promptText: How does Kafka's idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) prevent a retried send from creating a duplicate message on a single partition?
options: The broker deduplicates using the producer's PID and a per-partition monotonically increasing sequence number
The transaction coordinator writes a commit marker before allowing any retry
The consumer group filters duplicate offsets before delivering records to the application
The schema registry rejects any message it has already validated once
explanation: Kafka assigns each idempotent producer a Producer ID and stamps every message with an increasing sequence number per partition, so if a retry resends a message the broker already has, it recognizes the same PID and sequence number and drops the duplicate.

promptText: What is the key semantic difference between a KStream and a KTable in Kafka Streams?
options: A KStream treats every record as an independent fact; a KTable treats a new record for an existing key as an update that replaces the previous value
A KStream is backed by RocksDB while a KTable is held only in memory
A KStream requires co-partitioning to be created, while a KTable never does
A KStream can only be produced by Kafka Connect, while a KTable can only come from a compacted topic
explanation: A KStream has append-only insert semantics where two records with the same key are two separate events, while a KTable has upsert/changelog semantics representing current state per key, where a new record for an existing key overwrites it.

promptText: How does log compaction (cleanup.policy=compact) differ from ordinary time or size-based retention?
options: Compaction guarantees at least the latest record per key is retained indefinitely, regardless of age, rather than deleting whole segments once they age out
Compaction deletes all records older than a configured number of days, exactly like time-based retention but applied per partition
Compaction only applies to topics with a single partition, while retention applies to any partition count
Compaction removes duplicate messages sent by different producers within the same time window
explanation: Compaction is per-key, not time-based: a key updated once and never touched again survives every compaction pass indefinitely, while time/size retention discards whole segments once they age out or the partition exceeds a size cap regardless of key.

promptText: Why is Testcontainers generally preferred over embedded Kafka for integration tests that verify partitioning, rebalancing, or transactional behavior?
options: Testcontainers runs an actual production Kafka broker binary in a container, eliminating the risk that an in-process embedded broker behaves subtly differently
Testcontainers starts faster because it avoids the JVM in-process broker startup overhead entirely
Embedded Kafka cannot run more than one partition per topic, making it unsuitable for any partitioning test
Testcontainers does not require Docker, making it easier to run in any CI environment
explanation: Testcontainers spins up a real, containerized Kafka broker that behaves identically to production because it is the same broker binary, whereas embedded Kafka trades that fidelity for faster in-process startup and can drift from real broker behavior across versions.

promptText: Why is acks=all alone not sufficient to guarantee durability across a broker failure, requiring min.insync.replicas as well?
options: Because "all of the ISR" can shrink to just the leader during an outage, so acks=all could be satisfied by a single broker with no real redundancy
Because acks=all only applies to the first message in a batch, leaving later messages in the batch unacknowledged
Because acks=all disables the idempotent producer's sequence-number deduplication
Because acks=all requires every broker in the cluster to acknowledge, not just replicas of that partition, making it impractical to enforce
explanation: acks=all waits for every replica currently in the ISR, but if the ISR has shrunk to just the leader, that is the entire acknowledgement requirement; min.insync.replicas sets a floor below which the leader rejects writes with NotEnoughReplicasException instead of accepting them with false confidence.

promptText: A Kafka Streams instance running a stateful aggregation crashes and is rescheduled onto a new node. Why is the aggregation's state not actually lost, even though its RocksDB files were on the old node's local disk?
options: Every write to the local RocksDB state store is also written to an internal, compacted changelog topic in Kafka, so a new instance can rebuild the state store by replaying that topic
Kafka Streams automatically replicates RocksDB files to every broker in the cluster using the same replication factor as the source topic
RocksDB itself is a distributed database, so the state is still accessible from any node in the cluster
The state is recomputed by re-reading the original input topic from the very beginning every time any instance restarts
explanation: RocksDB is a fast local cache, not the source of truth; Kafka's replicated changelog topic is, so a crashed instance can rebuild its state store from the changelog, or fail over to a warm standby replica that already mirrors it.

promptText: Why do many production systems deliberately choose "effectively-once" (at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers) over wrapping every message in a Kafka transaction for true exactly-once semantics?
options: Wrapping every message in its own transaction adds real coordination overhead and can cut throughput by 20-50%, and the guarantee still would not extend past Kafka's own boundary anyway
Kafka transactions are deprecated in favor of idempotent consumers and will be removed in a future version
Idempotent consumers provide stronger guarantees than Kafka transactions in every scenario
Transactions only work with Avro-serialized messages, so JSON payloads require the effectively-once approach
explanation: Transactions require coordination with the transaction coordinator and commit markers on every partition, adding latency and reducing throughput, while still not covering side effects on external systems outside Kafka; effectively-once gets the same observable no-duplicate-effect behavior more cheaply and even covers non-Kafka systems.

promptText: Under BACKWARD schema compatibility mode in a schema registry, which change is safe to make to an Avro schema?
options: Adding a new field that has a default value
Renaming an existing field without using an Avro alias
Removing a field that never had a default value
Changing a field's type from string to int without any transition period
explanation: BACKWARD compatibility means new schema versions can read data written with the old schema; adding a field is safe only if it has a default (so old data lacking it still deserializes), while renaming without an alias looks like a remove-plus-add and removing a field without a prior default breaks that guarantee.

promptText: How does the cooperative sticky rebalancing protocol reduce the "stop the world" disruption seen under the original eager protocol?
options: It only revokes the specific partitions that actually need to move to a different consumer, letting consumers keep processing the partitions they already own
It eliminates rebalancing entirely by permanently pinning partitions to the first consumer that ever claimed them
It increases session.timeout.ms so consumers are never considered dead in the first place
It moves partition assignment logic from the group leader to the Kafka broker's controller
explanation: Under eager rebalancing every consumer revokes all of its partitions before any reassignment happens, stopping the whole group; cooperative sticky rebalancing computes the target assignment first and revokes only the partitions that are actually moving, so most of the group keeps consuming throughout.

promptText: At production scale, what is the main scaling failure that causes teams to migrate a saga from choreography to orchestration?
options: The business process only exists as the sum of scattered event handlers across many services, making it impossible to see or safely modify the overall workflow in one place
Choreography cannot technically support more than three services participating in a single saga
Kafka enforces a hard limit on the number of consumer groups that can subscribe to the same topic
Orchestration is always faster at runtime because it uses synchronous calls instead of events
explanation: With many steps, choreography's logic becomes implicit workflow sprawl spread across every service's event handlers, making it impossible to answer "where is this saga right now" without reconstructing a flowchart from scattered code; orchestration concentrates that visibility into one place at the cost of the orchestrator becoming a critical, stateful component.

promptText: A single customer key is generating far more Kafka traffic than any other key, concentrating load on one consumer. If strict per-key ordering genuinely must be preserved for every event under that key, which remediation is correct, and why does the alternative fail?
options: Keep the key unsalted and parallelize the actual downstream processing after the ordered consume, because salting the key would spread it across partitions and break the ordering guarantee
Apply key salting (append a hash-based suffix) so the key spreads across multiple partitions, since this preserves ordering while adding parallelism
Increase the topic's partition count immediately, since more partitions always resolve any hot-key imbalance regardless of ordering requirements
Switch the topic's cleanup.policy to compact, which automatically rebalances traffic away from hot keys
explanation: Salting a key to spread it across partitions explicitly sacrifices per-key ordering across the salted sub-keys, so if ordering truly matters the only viable fix is making the single ordered consumer's downstream work faster by parallelizing it after the ordered read, not before; adding partitions alone does nothing if the hot key still hashes to one partition.

promptText: Two separate incidents both show the same symptom in broker logs: repeated JoinGroup/SyncGroup cycles and climbing consumer lag. In one, a thread dump shows the consumer thread blocked on a downstream payment-gateway call; in the other, a thread dump during the same stall shows the poll thread simply not runnable at all. What does the second signature indicate, and how should it be fixed differently from the first?
options: The JVM itself is paused in a stop-the-world garbage collection cycle exceeding max.poll.interval.ms, requiring heap sizing and collector tuning rather than fixing a slow external call
Both signatures indicate the exact same root cause and should be fixed identically by raising max.poll.interval.ms permanently
The second signature means the broker's controller has failed over, which is fixed by restarting the entire consumer group
The second signature indicates a network partition between broker and ZooKeeper, fixed by switching the cluster to KRaft mode
explanation: A thread blocked in I/O points to a slow downstream call as the root cause, but a poll thread that is not runnable at all because the JVM itself froze during a GC pause is a heap-sizing or garbage collector problem; both produce identical rebalance-storm symptoms from the broker's perspective, so distinguishing them requires checking GC logs alongside the thread dump, and the fix (JVM tuning versus fixing the call) is different in each case.

promptText: A transactional Kafka producer restarts after a slow shutdown, but the old instance is still alive somewhere on the network and may still try to write. Which mechanism specifically prevents this old "zombie" instance from committing data, and how does it differ from the PID-plus-sequence-number mechanism?
options: The transaction coordinator bumps the producer epoch on every re-initialization of the same transactional.id and fences off any earlier epoch, whereas PID-plus-sequence-number only dedups retries from the same live producer instance
PID-plus-sequence-number already handles zombie fencing on its own, so no additional mechanism is needed once idempotence is enabled
The consumer's isolation.level=read_committed setting is what fences off the zombie producer by refusing to read anything from it
A randomly generated transactional.id on every restart ensures the old instance can never be confused with the new one
explanation: PID and sequence number dedup retries from the same producer instance on one partition, but preventing an old instance of that producer from writing at all after a newer instance has taken over requires producer epoch fencing tied to a stable transactional.id; using a fresh random transactional.id per restart would actually defeat this fencing because the new instance would no longer be recognized as a newer incarnation of the same producer.
